output:
Three things self-hosting exposed

Each of these presented as a symptom that pointed somewhere other than its cause. If you are standing up your own deployment and one of these bites you, this is what it actually was.

OneEvery call returns unauthorized, and your signature is fine

Symptom
unauthorized on every MCP call, from the first one. Looks like a broken signature or a mangled key.
Actual cause
The client had this deployment's URL baked in as its default base URL. Your key is correct; it is being presented to somebody else's host, which has never seen it.
Fix
Fixed upstream. The instance now substitutes its own URL when it serves the client file, the way /cli already did. A client downloaded from your deployment now talks to your deployment.

This only reached people who followed /start by hand rather than taking the generated command, so it stayed invisible for as long as there was exactly one host. The misdirection is that authentication failures train you to look at the credential. Here the credential was never the variable — the address was.

How to tell in ten seconds: check the base URL your installed client is actually using. If it is not your hostname, you have this bug, and no amount of key regeneration will move it.

TwoThe claude mcp add command on /start arrives as one joined line

Symptom
The copyable setup command renders without its line breaks, and without the backslashes that were supposed to be there.
Actual cause
A lone trailing backslash inside a JavaScript template literal is a line continuation, not a literal backslash. The escape consumed itself and the newline, silently.
Fix
Escape it — \\ — or build the command from an array joined on " \\\n".
// what was written — the backslash and the newline both vanish
const cmd = `claude mcp add sirdocalot \
  --transport http \
  https://example.invalid/mcp`;

// what it becomes
"claude mcp add sirdocalot   --transport http   https://example.invalid/mcp"

The output is still a runnable command, which is why nobody noticed for a while. It is just not the formatted, readable one that was intended.

The tell is that nothing errors. Template literals do not warn about this, and the resulting string is plausible. If a multi-line snippet in your own UI has collapsed, look for the continuation before you look at your renderer or your CSS white-space.

ThreeMAX_AWAIT_MS=90s quietly became 90 seconds

Symptom
A numeric environment variable appeared to be ignored. Timeouts behaved as though the setting had never been applied.
Actual cause
The value was unparseable — 90s is not a number of milliseconds — so the loader fell back to its default and said nothing. Setting it to a bad value and not setting it at all were indistinguishable from outside.
Fix
Fixed upstream. The loader now refuses loudly on an unparseable numeric variable instead of falling through to the default.

This one is worth naming precisely because of where it lived: a config loader whose entire stated posture is refusing loudly rather than guessing. A silent fallback inside a strict loader is worse than a silent fallback inside a permissive one, because you have been told you can trust the loader to shout, so you stop checking.

If you are writing one of these: a default is for an absent value. A present-but-invalid value is an operator error and should stop the process. Those are two different states and they should not share a code path.

And one that was not self-hosting: .label

Separately, a guard now exists that no page stylesheet redefines a class the shared stylesheet defines. This has bitten twice, both times caught by eye, which is not a method.

The most recent instance: the gallery defined .label. That is also what the block renderer calls a field label. Every input inside a preview rendered uppercase and tiny. The symptom looked like a broken preview renderer; the cause was a name collision two files away.

The guard is a test, and it was proved to bite — introduced against the known collision and watched to fail — before it was trusted. A collision test that has never been seen to fail is not a test, it is a reassurance.

Three of the four are fixed in the deployment; the collision guard is a test, not a fix, and will keep the fourth from recurring. All four presented at a distance from their cause, which is the only reason they are written down together.
